Original Article
Age-dependent changes in the dynamic functional
organization of the brain at rest: a cross-cultural
replication approach
Xi Yang 1, Xinqi Zhou 2, Fei Xin3, Benjamin Becker4,
*, David Linden1, Dennis Hernaus1,
*
1Department of Psychiatry & Neuropsychology, School for Mental Health and NeuroScience MHeNS, Maastricht University, Minderbroedersberg 4-6, 6211 LK
Maastricht, The Netherlands,
2Institute of Brain and Psychological Sciences, Sichuan Normal University, 610066 Chengdu, Sichuan, China,
3School of Psychology, Shenzhen University, 518060 Shenzhen, Guangdong, China,
4The Center of Psychosomatic Medicine, Sichuan Provincial Center for Mental Health, Sichuan Provincial People’s Hospital, University of Electronic Science and
Technology of China, Xiyuan Ave, West Hi-Tech Zone, 611731 Chengdu, Sichuan, China

Age-associated changes in brain function play an important role in the development of neurodegenerative diseases. Although previous
work has examined age-related changes in static functional connectivity, accumulating evidence suggests that advancing age is
especially associated with alterations in the dynamic interactions and transitions between different brain states, which hitherto have
received less attention. Conclusions of previous studies in this domain are moreover limited by suboptimal replicability of resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) and culturally homogenous cohorts. Here, we investigate the robustness of age-associated changes in dynamic functional connectivity (dFC) by capitalizing on the availability of fMRI cohorts from two cultures
(Western European and Chinese). In both the LEMON (Western European) and SALD (Chinese) cohorts, we consistently identify two
distinct states: a more frequent segregated within-network connectivity state (state I) and a less frequent integrated between-network
connectivity state (state II). Moreover, in both these cohorts, older (55–80 years) compared to younger participants (20–35 years) exhibited
lower occurrence of and spent less time in state I. Older participants also tended to exhibit more transitions between networks and
greater variance in global efficiency. Overall, our cross-cultural replication of age-associated changes in dFC metrics implies that advancing age is robustly associated with a reorganization of dynamic brain activation that favors the use of less functionally specific networks.

Primary cohort
As a primary cohort, we selected the LEMON (http://fcon_1000.
projects.nitrc.org/indi/retro/MPI_LEMON.html) study (Babayan
et al. 2019). This dataset comprised 228 native German adults,
which included both healthy participants and participants
with (current) psychiatric or neurological disorders. Given the
sensitivity of dFC to head motion (Preti et al. 2017), we employed
stringent head motion criteria (max. head motion >3 mm
translational, >3◦ rotation; n = 3). We additionally excluded
participants (i) that were taking psychoactive drugs (urine drug
screening and semi-structured interview for buprenorphine,
amphetamines, benzodiazepines, cocaine, methamphetamine,
morphine/heroine, methadone, and marihuana; n = 19), (ii) with
neurological disorders (DSM-5 diagnosis; n = 28) and/or alcohol
abuse and family history of alcohol addiction (DSM-5 diagnosis
and semi-structured interview; n = 53), (iii) with failed spatial
normalization as identified by visual inspection (n = 2), and (iv)
with missing demographic and/or MRI data (n = 8). After applying
these criteria, a total of 133 participants remained. In line
with previous studies (Doucet et al. 2021), and to investigate
age-associated changes in dFC metrics, subjects from both
datasets were subdivided into young and older groups (young:
n = 88, age range = 20–35, male/female = 57/31; older: n = 45, age
range = 55–80, male/female = 22/23). All participants provided
written informed consent. The study was approved by the Ethics
Committee of the Medical Faculty at the University of Leipzig,
Germany.

Cross-cultural replication cohort
As a cross-cultural replication sample, we used the publicly
accessible Southwest University Adult Lifespan Dataset (SALD;
http://fcon_1000.projects.nitrc.org/indi/retro/sald.html) resting-state fMRI dataset consisting of 494 healthy native Chinese
adults (Wei et al. 2018). In this dataset, participants with a
(current) psychiatric and/or neurological disorder and/or the
use of psychotropic drugs within 3 months of the MRI scan
were deemed ineligible (and were therefore not included in the
dataset). We excluded 163 participants based on head motion
(max. head motion >3 mm translation, >3◦ rotation; n = 16),
failed spatial normalization as defined by visual inspection
(n = 21), ages that fell outside of the age ranges of the young
and older LEMON participants (n = 127), and missing fMRI data
(n = 1). Please note that some participants fit multiple exclusion
criteria: the numbers reported here therefore reflect the number
of participants that met each exclusion criterion. Three hundred
thirty subjects were included for further data analysis (young:
n = 168, age range = 20–35, male/female = 68/100; older: n = 162,
age range = 55–80, male/female = 66/96). All participants provided
written informed consent. The study was approved by the
Research Ethics Committee of the Brain Center of Southwest
University.

fMRI acquisition
Primary cohort
MRI data were collected on a 3 Tesla MRI system (MAGNETOM
Verio, Siemens Healthcare GmbH, Erlangen, Germany) equipped
with a 32-channel head coil. Structural T1-weighted images were
acquired using a magnetization-prepared 2 rapid acquisition
gradient echo (MP2RAGE) (Marques et al. 2010) sequence
(repetition time [TR] = 5,000 ms, echo time [TE] = 2.92 ms, flip
angle [FA] 1 = 4◦, FA 2 = 5◦, field of view [FOV] = 256 mm, voxel
size = 1 × 1 × 1 mm). Resting-state data were acquired using a T2∗-
weighted echo planar imaging (EPI) sequence with the following
parameters: TR = 1,400 ms, TE = 30 ms, FA = 69◦, FOV = 202 mm,
voxel size =2.3 × 2.3 × 2.3 mm, slice thickness = 2.3 mm, image
matrix = 88 × 88. The resting state scan duration in this cohort was
15 min 30s. During the scan, participants were asked to keep their
eyes open and to remain awake while looking at a low-contrast
fixation cross.

Cross-cultural replication sample (validation cohort)
All SALD MRI data were collected on a 3 Tesla MRI system
(Siemens Magnetom Trio, Siemens Medical, Erlangen, Germany)
equipped with a 16-channel whole-brain coil. Structural data were
acquired using a magnetization-prepared rapid gradient echo
(MPRAGE) sequence (TR = 1,900 ms, TE =2.52 ms, FA =9◦, FOV =176,
and voxel size = 1 × 1 × 1 mm). FMRI data were acquired using a
gradient echo planar image (GRE-EPI) sequence (TR = 2,000 ms,
TE = 30 ms, FA = 90◦, FOV = 220 mm, voxel size = 3.4 × 3.4 × 4 mm,
slice thickness = 3 mm, image matrix = 64 × 64). The total acquisition time was 8 min 4 s (242 volumes). Participants were instructed
to remain awake with their eyes closed and to rest without
thinking of anything. The SALD team excluded participants who
fell asleep during the scan.

fMRI data analysis
MRI data preprocessing
All resting-state fMRI data were preprocessed in a combined
SPM12 (http://www.fil.ion.ac.uk/spm/; Wellcome Trust Centre for
Neuroimaging) and DPABI (Version: V4.3_200401; http://rfmri.org/
dpabi) (Yan et al. 2016) analysis pipeline. We discarded the first 5
volumes to ensure MRI signal equilibrium. Since scan duration
can influence resting-state connectivity estimates (Birn et al.
2013), we discarded the last 312 volumes of resting-state data
for participants in the LEMON dataset, resulting in a scan duration (7 min 56 s, 340 volumes) that was nearly identical to the
scan duration of the SALD dataset (note: we repeated our dFC
analyses using the entire time series, see Temporal properties
section). Next, all images were corrected for head motion, spatial normalization using the Diffeomorphic Anatomical Registration Through Exponentiated Lie Algebra (DARTEL) template, after
which the resulting images were smoothed (6 mm full-width at
half-maximum Gaussian kernel). We discuss band-pass filtering
as part of the dFC procedures reported below (see Computation of
dFC section).
Comparing head motion as defined by framewise displacements (Jenkinson et al. 2002), we observed a significant difference between the young and older groups in the LEMON (young:
mean ± SD = 0.11 ± 0.03; older: mean ± SD = 0.18 ± 0.08; P < 0.001,
two-sample T-test) and SALD dataset (young: mean ± SD = 0.08 ±
0.04; older: mean ± SD = 0.15 ± 0.07; P < 0.001, two-sample T-test).
We therefore included 24 motion parameters (6 motion parameters of the current volume and the preceding volume, plus each
of these values squared) for each participant. Since global signal
regression can introduce spurious anti-correlations which may
reduce the sensitivity of dFC (Murphy et al. 2009; Anderson,
Druzgal, et al. 2011a; Anderson, Harris, et al. 2011b; Saad et al.
2012), we used a component-based noise reduction method (CompCor: 5 principal components) to remove noise from white matter
(WM), cerebrospinal fluid (CSF), global signal, and other sources of
physiological noise (Behzadi et al. 2007; Chai et al. 2012). CompCor
is a commonly used technique (Kim et al. 2017; Díez-Cirarda et al.
2018) that is thought to have greater specificity and sensitivity for
positive correlations (compared to, e.g. global signal regression),
as well as a lower risk of artificially introducing anticorrelations
into FC estimations.

Group independent component analysis
Next, group-level ICA was performed using the Group ICA Of fMRI
Toolbox (GIFT) (http://icatb.sourceforge.net/) (Calhoun et al. 2001)
with the aim of identifying networks of interest. Before performing
data reduction, voxel-wise variance normalization steps were
applied as recommended by Allen et al. (2011), which is useful for
high-dimensionality reduction (Beckmann and Smith 2004). For
subject-specific data reduction, a total of 120 principal components were retained using principal component analysis. For the
group-level data reduction, the concatenated (reduced) subject-level data were decomposed into 100 group independent components (ICs) using the expectation maximization algorithm. The
Infomax ICA algorithm was repeated 20 times in ICASSO (http://
www.cis.hut.fi/projects/ica/icasso) to improve stability (Himberg
et al. 2004). Components with an average intra-cluster similarity
value >0.8 were retained (Kim et al. 2017). To obtain subject-specific spatial maps and time courses for each IC, group ICs
were backprojected using the GICA back reconstruction algorithm
(Calhoun et al. 2001). Spatial maps and time courses of components were not scale since we opted for a variance normalization
method during data preprocessing (Calhoun et al. 2001).

Computation of dFC
DFC was estimated using the GIFT toolbox via 2 steps: (i) a
sliding window approach (i.e. changes in FC over time) and (ii) K-means clustering (i.e. recurrence of FC activity patterns). Resting-state time series were divided into bins of 40/28 TRs (LEMON:
40∗1.4 = 56 s; SALD: 28∗2 = 56 s) with sigma 3-TR of Gaussian,
and a 1 TR step between windows. Additional processing steps
were applied to improve the signal-to-noise ratio and remove
physiological confounders. Those steps included detrending (linear, cubic, and quadratic), regression of motion parameters and
physiological noise including WM, CSF, and other physiological
noises (total of 29 regressors), despiking using 3DDESPIKE and
low-pass filtering using a high-frequency cutoff of 0.15 Hz.
Next, we utilized the average sliding window correlation
(ASWC) to improve the robustness of correlation coefficient
estimations and to minimize the loss of temporal resolution
(compared to e.g. a sliding window correlation approach). ASWC
averages a predefined number of consecutive sliding window
correlations (SWCs) and then advances one step and averages the
next set of SWCs for dFC (22 s window length), which resulted in
284 (LEMON) and 198 (SALD) final correlation matrices containing
C2
51=1275 (LEMON) and C2
43=903 (SALD) component pairs (Vergara
et al. 2019). A penalty on the L1 norm was imposed in the graphic
LASSO framework with 100 repetitions to promote sparsity in
estimation (Friedman et al. 2008). We selected a 56 s segmented
window length based on previous work indicating that window
lengths between 30 and 60 s successfully capture resting-state
dFC fluctuations and do not yield substantially different results,
which, moreover, allowed us to match the window length of the
LEMON dataset to the SALD dataset (Preti et al. 2017). To our
knowledge, no gold standard exists for window length in dFC
analyses. To nevertheless ascertain that our results were robust
to variations in window length, we repeated our analyses of dFC
states using two additional commonly-used window lengths (30–
40s: Lemon: 25TR ∗ 1.4 = 35 s, SALD: 17TR ∗ 2 = 34 s; 40–50s: Lemon:
35TR ∗ 1.4 = 49 s, SALD: 22TR ∗ 2 = 44 s, see Temporal properties
section). Sex was included as a covariate in the estimation. Finally,
all resulting FC matrices were transformed to z-scores using
Fisher’s z-transformation.

Dynamic topological metrics: global and local efficiency
difference between 2 groups
We used GRETNA (http:/www.nitrc.org/projects/Gretna) to obtain
topological properties of the resting-state fMRI data. Brain aging is
thought to affect two key graph metrics that control network efficiency: global and local efficiency (Kim et al. 2017; Xia et al. 2019).
Global network efficiency was defined as the average efficiency
across all node pairs, representing parallel information transfer
in the network. In comparison, local efficiency was defined as the
average of nodal local efficiency within neighbors of a node, which
is thought to represent communication among neighbors.
LEMON and SALD ICs were defined as nodes and the FC
between components as edges for each time window. Subject-specific FC matrices were then binarized with respect to sparsity
threshold (i.e. the number of actual edges divided by the
maximum possible number of edges). The sparsity threshold was
defined as 0.1–0.34 in 0.01 increments to maximize the reliability
of the global and local efficiency estimation. In line with previous
work (Kim et al. 2017), only positive correlations were included
in this study. Next, we obtained the global and local efficiency
at each sparsity threshold. We applied an area under the curve
approach to avoid the selection of an arbitrary threshold (Kim
et al. 2017; Navalpotro-Gomez et al. 2020; Xu et al. 2021). Finally,
as suggested by Kim et al. (2017), we calculated the variance of the
global and local efficiency over time to examine age-associated
differences in dynamic graph properties and compared young
and older participants on these metrics using Wilcoxon rank-sum
tests.

Data and materials availability
All fMRI data included in this study are publicly available
(LEMON dataset: http://fcon_1000.projects.nitrc.org/indi/retro/
MPI_LEMON.html) and (SALD dataset: http://fcon_1000.projects.
nitrc.org/indi/retro/sald.html). The dFC results of the current
study have been uploaded to the Open Science Framework
(https://osf.io/xenpc/).
